title: Managing with Style: The Effect of Managers on Firm Policies
research_question: Do individual top managers systematically shape firm investment, financial, and organizational policies and performance, beyond what firm- and industry-level factors explain? Are observable managerial traits such as age/birth cohort and MBA education associated with distinct patterns in corporate decision-making?
data_description: The authors construct a manager-firm matched panel data set tracking top executives (CEOs, CFOs, and other top officers such as COOs and division presidents) across multiple firms over time. Manager names come from the Forbes 800 files (1969–1999) and Standard & Poor's Execucomp data (1992–1999, top-five highest paid executives at ~1,500 firms). The sample is restricted to firms employing at least one executive observed in at least one other firm with a minimum three-year stay, yielding roughly 600 firms and over 500 mobile managers. Annual firm-level accounting variables (capital expenditures, Tobin's Q, cash flow, leverage, interest coverage, cash holdings, dividends, R&D, advertising, SG&A, acquisitions, return on assets) come from COMPUSTAT and SDC Platinum. Governance information is from CDA Spectrum. CEO birth year and MBA status are hand-collected from the S&P Directory of Corporate Executives and Who's Who of Corporate America. Banks, insurance, and utilities are excluded.
institutional_context: The setting is large publicly traded U.S. corporations during 1969–1999, a period in which executive mobility across firms was common: in the broader Execucomp universe, only about 48 percent of CEOs were internal promotions, and a large share of inter-firm transitions cross two-digit industry boundaries (63 percent for CEO-to-CEO moves, 71 percent for CFO-to-CFO moves). The business press and managers themselves often portray top executives as imprinting personal 'styles' on firms—e.g., differing in propensities toward acquisitions, diversification, leverage, dividends, R&D, or cost-cutting. Standard corporate finance research, however, typically attributes cross-sectional variation in firm policy to firm- and industry-level fundamentals, leaving substantial unexplained heterogeneity. The mobility of executives between firms with different histories, technologies, and governance structures provides a rich setting in which to ask whether the identity of the person at the top, separate from firm characteristics, helps account for corporate behavior.
